dialogue.shona: Dandemutande rakagara pasi. Rine makumbo akawanda, rine makushe uye rine mavara matema neebhurauni.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakagara')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakagara' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('mavara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'mavara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Spiders ('Dandemutande') in Shona Folklore & Idiom
cultural_notes.content: The word 'dandemutande' refers both to a spider and to its intricate web (and in modern Shona, even the internet/World Wide Web!). Large harmless baboon spiders with hairy legs ('makushe') are a familiar sight in rural woodlands during the rainy season.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this sentence about tree leaves: 'Mashizha emuti uyu ane ruvara ______.' (The leaves of this tree have a green colour.)

Which bus goes to the city centre?

active_exercises.explanation: 'Mukoma wangu' = 'My older brother', 'akatenga' = 'bought', 'mota chena' = 'a white car', 'nezuro' = 'yesterday'.

active_exercises.prompt: Your friend just passed her driving test! What do you say to congratulate her in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!' and 'nekubudirira kwako' means 'on your success'.
